rationale: B wins by being a little less in love with the angle and a little more alert to what can kill it. Its best line is the discipline in “the angle survives as detect-and-respond, not as improvement,” while A’s “now reacts to snoring by changing the bed’s temperature” is punchier but edges closer to an unproven causal claim. Both sets are real strategic material; B is just cleaner about the traps before a reporter finds them first.
gaps_in_A: “now reacts to snoring by changing the bed's temperature” overstates the supplied fact unless Eight Sleep can prove the adjustment is triggered by snoring, not merely happening alongside sensing.
“a low SpO2 reading overnight and changes its own temperature in response” needs proof before it belongs in the angle; the update did not specify that low oxygen triggers the bed action.

“The sensors are in the cover. Knowing your blood oxygen costs the top subscription tier” is sharp, but the strongest consumer-rights version depends on whether existing owners already have the sensors. A flags this, but the headline reads more settled than the facts.
A misses B’s sharper audience mismatch question: Eight Sleep markets to athletes and biohackers, but snoring and SpO2 anxiety may point to a different buyer.
gaps_in_B: “This bed changes its temperature while you are doing it” is vivid, but still assumes a real-time snoring-triggered response that the update does not fully spell out.
“The question exists the moment the reading appears on a customer's phone” invents the phone/app surface. Probably true, still not in the supplied facts.
“Here is what it is measuring” promises study specifics the update does not provide; the proof section walks it back, but the headline is ahead of the evidence.

“The product costs several thousand dollars. Eight Sleep is privately held” are true facts, but the privately held point is decorative in the subscription angle unless tied to pricing opacity, margins, or investor pressure.
